Parents are being urged to consider postponing sending their sons to traditional initiation schools this summer as authorities prepare for extreme heat and other weather-related risks.
Speaking to CapeTalk/702's Africa Melane, Mtetho Sithonga, an Environmental Health Practitioner at the Garden Route District Municipality's Knysna sub-office, said officials had been warned to prepare for very hot conditions, as well as the possibility of flooding and wildfires.
The warning has prompted the municipality to advise parents to consider postponing sending their children to initiation schools this summer.
“My call, I would suggest that the parents, if it's possible, please postpone to send your child to the bush this coming season because it's going to be extremely hot,” he said.
The municipality recently met with dozens of amakhankatha (traditional guardians) and others involved in Ulwaluko (initiation) to discuss preparations for the upcoming summer initiation season.
One concern is the material traditionally used to cover shelters at initiation schools.
Sithonga said plastic coverings could trap heat and restrict airflow during extremely hot weather.
“It's going to be extremely hot and those plastics, they don't allow penetration of the air easily. We need to change the things that we use to make amaboma... so that the air can move easily inside the amaboma.”
He suggested using a more breathable material, such as linen, with plastic coverings added only when it rains and removed afterwards.

Contralesa bemoans deaths of 35 initiates as ‘killing the leaders of tomorrow’
Where initiation schools are located will also be important.
Sithonga warned that some shelters were traditionally built on slopes or in areas vulnerable to heavy rain, flooding or wildfires.
He said initiation schools should operate only at sites that were registered and known to local municipalities.
“Only use the places that are registered and known by everybody in the area.”
Knowing exactly where schools are located is particularly important if emergency services need to evacuate initiates, he said.
Sithonga said traditional leaders and caregivers who attended the recent meeting had responded well to the safety recommendations.
“We have to keep this tradition going forward and we need to make sure that there is no incident that can be prevented to take place at those schools.”

Thai Banking Stocks Plunge Amid Potential Impacts From Flood Relief Measures
On Wednesday at 11:45 AM (Bangkok time), the share price of Kasikornbank Public Company Limited (SET: KBANK) dropped by 3.72% or THB 9.00 to THB 233.00, with a trading value of THB 6.07 billion.
Krung Thai Bank Public Company Limited (SET: KTB) lost 4.62% or THB 2.00 to THB 41.25, with a trading value of THB 5.75 billion.
Bangkok Bank Public Company Limited (SET: BBL) contracted by 1.85% or THB 3.50 to THB 185.50, with a trading value of THB 2.04 billion.
SCB X Public Company Limited (SET: SCB) declined by 2.29% or THB 3.50 to THB 149.50, with a trading value of THB 2.09 billion.
TMBThanachart Bank Public Company Limited (SET: TTB) fell by 2.00% or THB 0.06 to THB 2.94, with a trading value of THB 1.07 billion.
Kiatnakin Phatra Bank Public Company Limited (SET: KKP) slumped by 2.67% or THB 3.00 to THB 109.50, with a trading value of THB 796.74 million.
KGI Securities (Thailand) wrote that, in response to the recent flooding, several commercial banks have introduced relief measures to support customers in both retail and SME loan segments. These measures include temporary suspension of interest payments for three to six months, reduction of principal repayments, lowering of monthly installment amounts, extension of debt repayment periods, and offering special interest rates.
For SME customers, most banks are providing additional support measures, such as offering extra working capital loans and special interest-rate loans at approximately 3.5%. Combined with assistance from state-owned specialized financial institutions, these are expected to offer comprehensive support to debtors nationwide.
Additionally, the brokerage anticipates that non-bank companies will gradually roll out similar relief programs in line with commercial banks in the near future. In terms of operational impacts, the support measures for retail customers may put pressure on the net interest margin of banks.
KTB is expected to be most impacted, given its high proportion of retail customers at 40% of total loans, followed by SCB at 15%, KBANK at 10%, and BBL at less than 10%.
However, KGI believes that these measures present an opportunity for banks to accelerate debt restructuring, which should ultimately help reduce pressure on credit costs, in line with forecasts for 2026. The estimated credit costs are 1.04% for KTB, 1.24% for BBL, 1.50% for KBANK, and 1.62% for SCB.
Regarding investment outlook, KGI maintains an ‘Overweight’ recommendation on the banking sector despite recent share price declines and underperformance relative to the SET Index. The impact of the flooding on the overall economy and GDP growth is assessed as manageable. Consequently, the recent dip in bank stock prices is regarded as a buying opportunity, with the brokerage highlighting KBANK, KTB, KKP, and TTB as its top picks, all recommended as ‘Buy’.

Paris and the Île-de-France region are placed under yellow storm alert this Wednesday, September 30, 2026, joining 54 departments across France. The forecast calls for gray skies, scattered rain and gusty winds, ahead of a welcome clearing on Thursday afternoon.
A new backdrop overhead. In its latest bulletin, Météo-France places Paris and the Île-de-France region under a yellow thunderstorm alert for this Wednesday, September 30, 2026. The eight departments of the Île-de-France area are affected: Paris (75), Seine-et-Marne (77), Yvelines (78), Essonne (91), Hauts-de-Seine (92), Seine-Saint-Denis (93), Val-de-Marne (94) and Val-d'Oise (95).
Rain, scattered thunderstorms and gusty winds will punctuate the day, ahead of a sunny lull on Thursday. Here's a briefing on the vigilance map and the weather forecast for Paris.
Which departments in the Île-de-France region are under yellow thunderstorm alert?
In Île-de-France, the map turns yellow from one end of the region to the other. Here are the Île-de-France departments affected:
To check the situation near you, Météo-France offers a weather‑vigilance map for Paris and the inner suburbs, as well as dedicated pages for Yvelines, Seine-et-Marne, Essonne and Val-d'Oise, updated every morning.
What’s the weather forecast for Paris this Wednesday, September 30?
The day opens under a thick blanket of clouds that won’t yield to the sun. Scattered showers are expected from early on, with temperatures around 20–21°C and a gentle southerly breeze.
In the afternoon, the rain sets in and the thermometer swings between 19 and 21°C. Showers could locally intensify into storms, bringing heavy downpours in a short time. Under the most active cells, the gusts of wind can reach 60 to 70 km/h.
The evening remains damp, with more rain and about 19°C. In the night from Wednesday to Thursday, the sky will thin out slightly, like a curtain just beginning to be drawn.
What will the weather be like in Paris on Thursday, October 1?
Thursday, a breezy westerly wind cools the morning air. By daybreak the sun remains hidden behind the clouds, and temperatures dip to between 16 and 18°C. A light jacket will come in handy as you head to work.
The scene changes in the afternoon. The soleil makes a strong comeback and the thermometer rises to between 20 and 22°C. In the evening, the sky clears a little more, with some sunshine, and temperatures between 19 and 21°C.
The improvement, however, looks like a mere pause. The weather will deteriorate again in the coming days, with cloudy skies and temperatures around 19°C. An early October that already feels like autumn has taken hold.
What alert levels are in place elsewhere in France?
Île-de-France isn’t the only region under this cloudy sky. In its latest bulletin, Météo-France places 54 departments on the list of yellow thunderstorm alerts for this Wednesday, stretching along a broad swath from the northern part of Aquitaine to Hauts-de-France. The affected departments include Aisne, Allier, Ardennes, Aube, Aveyron, Bouches-du-Rhône, Calvados, Cantal, Charente, Charente-Maritime, Cher, Corrèze, Côte-d’Or, Creuse, Dordogne, Drôme, Eure, Eure-et-Loir, Gironde, Indre, Indre-et-Loir, Loir-et-Cher, Loire, Haute-Loire, Loiret, Lot, Marne and Haute-Marne.
The list also includes Meuse, Nièvre, Nord, Oise, Orne, Pas-de-Calais, Puy-de-Dôme, Saône-et-Loire, Sarthe, Seine-Maritime, Deux-Sèvres, Somme, Tarn, Tarn-et-Garonne, Vaucluse, Vienne, Haute-Vienne, and Yonne.
The situation is markedly tenser in the south of the country. The Cévennes episode that started last night is intensifying over Languedoc and will persist throughout the day, with stormy rains spilling from the mountains into the plains. Météo-France is urging extreme caution: Gard and Hérault are placed under a red rain-flooding alert, while Ardèche and Lozère sit at orange alert level.
What does a yellow thunderstorm alert mean, and how can you stay safe?
Yellow is the first level of alert on Météo-France's scale. It signals weather phenomena that are common in the region, but which can occasionally become dangerous. No need to panic, but it's a good reason to keep an eye on the sky and on the forecasts.
When a thunderstorm hits, don’t take shelter under a tree and stay away from waterways. The safest option is to move into a sturdy building. On the road, slow down and never drive onto a flooded stretch. Also secure any items that could be whipped around on balconies (pots, parasols, light furniture), as 70 km/h gusts are enough to send them flying.
Météo-France outlines the best practices on its page dedicated to dangers related to thunderstorms, and the Pluies intenses service flags the most significant episodes, listed commune by commune. On the travel front, a quick check of the RATP, Transilien, and Bison Futé sites helps anticipate any slowdowns.
What to do in Paris on a rainy day?
This Wednesday, put away the picnic baskets and park strolls. If a thunderstorm rolls in, it’s wiser to postpone outdoor outings. Paris and the Île-de-France region thankfully offer plenty of indoor refuges to ride out the shower: museums, temporary exhibitions, cinemas, or the covered passages of the 2nd arrondissement, such as Galerie Vivienne.
The City of Paris also offers a curated selection of free activities to enjoy on a rainy day, with several municipal museums open to the public at no charge. Also find our ideas for things to do in Paris on a rainy day and our pick of current exhibitions in Paris.

Africa’s Sahel region is projected to suffer the greatest loss of life from the heat brought on by this year’s strong El Niño. A belt of dry land stretching across Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, between the Sahara Desert in the north and tropical savannas in the south, the Sahel covers about 3.05 million square kilometres. It cuts through parts of Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad, Nigeria, Sudan, Senegal, and Eritrea.
Four countries in the region are projected to be affected the most by El Niño from September 2026 through to the end of February 2027: Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, and Chad.
In Nigeria, more than 60% of people were estimated to live below the national poverty line in 2025, while even homes connected to the grid face frequent power cuts. In Sudan, ongoing war has destroyed businesses and jobs while damaging power infrastructure, leaving an estimated 57% of the population in extreme poverty in 2025. In Niger, 41% lived below the national poverty line in 2021.
In Chad, 44.8% of the population lived in poverty in 2022. A vast majority in both countries depend on farming, leaving them critically exposed to severe droughts and poor harvests. Only 21% of people in Niger and 13% in Chad had access to electricity in 2024, leaving most without power to run even a basic cooling fan.
The projections show that these four countries will likely see 66,800 additional deaths from extreme heat compared with a normal year. Nearly half of these fatalities — 31,400 — are projected to occur in Nigeria, the most populous of the four with 237.5 million residents. This makes Nigeria the country most likely to suffer the highest heat mortality globally under this super El Niño.
Sudan is projected to record the second largest number of heat-related deaths at 17,500, followed by Niger with 10,000 and Chad with 8,000. Some of the highest temperature anomalies across the globe over the next six months will occur across the Sahel, explaining why the region faces far higher impacts from the super El Niño than other parts of the world.
The research also projects that heat-related deaths will generally be higher in impoverished regions than in wealthier areas facing similar temperatures. This includes countries across the Sahel, primarily because low-income communities have far fewer resources to protect their populations from extreme heat.

Natura is a long-term body of work that looks at how we change when the world is transformed around us. It does that through the stories of women who are deciding whether and how to foster life within it.
This project is both a long-term photography project supported by the National Geographic Society, and a feature-length documentary film, which follows four women, landscapes, and points along the spectrum of reproductive choice. Together, I hope these two sister projects will help widen our understanding of motherhood beyond biological birth, to what it means to care for, tend, heal, and defend the world we share, and how to do that in an age of burning. The heat and pregnancy story is one chapter of the photography series.
Part of what I'm trying to do is think about how we change as humans. And most studies show that intimate conversations across generations are much more likely to change us than politics and external data or research. We are more moved to change from our emotional settings than our cerebral. Natura is trying to find new ways to tell the climate story, and to do that through this most intimate and universal lens.
What do you hope people walk away from after seeing your photos of pregnancy and extreme heat?
I want people to feel connected to the women in the photos, to feel like they’re their neighbors, sisters, daughters. I felt very connected to the women that I worked with. I was a new mother myself while making this work, so none of it was abstract to me.
